title: The Disappearance of Ambrose Bierce
subtitle: Mexico · 1913
voice_instructions: Measured, quiet, a little hushed — calm and unhurried, but with a touch more forward energy than a long documentary; the cold voice of something that read the whole file. Never sensational. Small pauses.

beats.vo: At seventy-one, Ambrose Bierce, the writer they called Bitter Bierce, set out for revolutionary Mexico. He never came home.
beats.picture: Photograph of Ambrose Bierce dated 7 October 1892: seated, three-quarter length, thick swept-back hair and moustache, looking straight at the camera. (Landscape crop on his face and upper body.)

beats.vo: He reportedly went to travel with Pancho Villa's army as an observer.
beats.picture: Photograph, 1914 (Bain News Service, Library of Congress): General Pancho Villa on horseback, riding toward the camera at the head of his riders, dust, a wagon behind. (Commons category: Battle of Ojinaga, January 1914.)

beats.vo: His last known letter is dated Chihuahua, December twenty-sixth, nineteen thirteen. He was leaving, it said, for an unknown destination.
beats.picture: Photograph, 1913 (Library of Congress): Villa's troops passing through Chihuahua: horsemen in a city street watched by a crowd.

beats.vo: After that, nothing certain. Some say he was at Ojinaga, on the border, in January nineteen fourteen. Others say Sierra Mojada, or Marfa, Texas.
beats.picture: Photograph, 1914 (Library of Congress): "Federalists at Ojinaga, watching advance of rebels": Mexican federal soldiers standing on high ground, one with binoculars.

beats.vo: Civil War veteran, author of The Devil's Dictionary. Where and when he died has never been established.
beats.picture: Photograph of Bierce, published no later than 1911: older, seated, holding rolled papers, looking at the camera.

facts.claim: Bierce (born 24 June 1842) was 71 when he left Washington, D.C., in October 1913 on a journey that led toward revolutionary Mexico ('At seventy-one ... set out for revolutionary Mexico'); 'set out for' used instead of 'went into' because some doubt he ever crossed
He never returned ('He never came home'; Mental Floss: he never returned)
He reportedly joined / meant to travel with Pancho Villa's army as an observer (Wikipedia: 'joined Pancho Villa's army as an observer'; Lit Hub same; hedged with 'reportedly')

His last known letter, to Blanche Partington, is dated Chihuahua, 26 December 1913, and reads 'As to me, I leave here tomorrow for an unknown destination' (VO paraphrases; the letter itself is known only second-hand, which is why VO says 'last known')
No confirmed sightings after the last letter ('After that, nothing certain')

Theory: he was with Villa's army at Ojinaga, on the US border opposite Presidio, Texas, in January 1914 (one soldier reported seeing him with the army before the battle of 10/11 January 1914, not after)
Theory: Sierra Mojada, Coahuila (local oral tradition recorded by priest James Lienert)
Theory: an ill American calling himself 'Ambrosia' died of pneumonia 17 January 1914 and was buried at Marfa, Texas
Civil War veteran (9th Indiana Infantry, 1861-1866) and author of The Devil's Dictionary

The date and place of his death have never been established; fate remains a mystery as of 2026 (Wikipedia: 'Bierce's ultimate fate remains a mystery'; 2025 coverage still treats it as unsolved: Astonishing Legends Jan 2025, Reader's Digest list updated 2025)
Caption only: some doubt he ever entered Mexico (the trip as a ruse; Partington's Grand Canyon suicide theory)
